Hồ Chí Minh was the Vietnamese communist revolutionary who led Vietnam's fight for independence from France and founded the Democratic Republic of Vietnam, later North Vietnam, in 1945. He was its president from 1946 until his death in 1969.

He was born Nguyễn Sinh Cung in central Vietnam, then part of French Indochina, and used dozens of other names during his life. Much about his early years is uncertain. In 1911 he left Vietnam as a kitchen hand on a French ship and spent thirty years abroad, in France, Britain, the United States, the Soviet Union and China. In 1919, as Nguyễn Ái Quốc, he petitioned the powers at the Paris Peace Conference for Vietnamese rights. He was a founding member of the French Communist Party in 1920 and founded the Indochinese Communist Party in 1930.

The key steps of his career:

  • In 1941 he returned to Vietnam and founded the Việt Minh, a front to fight both Japan and France.
  • After Japan's surrender he led the August Revolution and declared independence in Hanoi on 2 September 1945, quoting the American Declaration of Independence. The famine of 1945 had just killed huge numbers in the north.
  • France fought to return. The Việt Minh won at Điện Biên Phủ in 1954, and Vietnam was split at the 17th parallel.
  • In the north his government carried out a violent land reform, and from 1959 it sent fighters and supplies south along the Ho Chi Minh trail.

He died during the Vietnam War, and became more a symbol than a ruler in his last years. When the north took Saigon in 1975 (Fall of Saigon), the city was renamed Hồ Chí Minh City.
